claim: A central theme that governs the functional design of biological networks is their ability to sustain stable function despite widespread parametric variability.
source: A central theme that governs the functional design of biological networks is their ability to sustain stable function despite widespread parametric variability.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological networks supported by the context of the study and established scientific understanding.

claim: Increasing degrees of biological heterogeneities progressively disrupted the emergence of grid-patterned activity in a two-dimensional continuous attractor network.
source: We show that increasing degrees of biological heterogeneities progressively disrupted the emergence of grid-patterned activity and resulted in progressively large perturbations in low-frequency neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from simulations shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Increasing degrees of biological heterogeneities resulted in progressively large perturbations in low-frequency neural activity.
source: We show that increasing degrees of biological heterogeneities progressively disrupted the emergence of grid-patterned activity and resulted in progressively large perturbations in low-frequency neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CAN models with resonating neurons were resilient to the incorporation of heterogeneities and exhibited stable grid-patterned firing.
source: Strikingly, CAN models with resonating neurons were resilient to the incorporation of heterogeneities and exhibited stable grid-patterned firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figures 8 and 11.

claim: CAN models with mechanistic resonators were more effective in targeted suppression of low-frequency activity than phenomenological resonators.
source: We found CAN models with mechanistic resonators to be more effective in targeted suppression of low-frequency activity, with the slow kinetics of the negative feedback loop essential in stabilizing these networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative spectral analysis data shown in Figure 13.

claim: The slow kinetics of the negative feedback loop was essential in stabilizing CAN networks with mechanistic resonators.
source: We found CAN models with mechanistic resonators to be more effective in targeted suppression of low-frequency activity, with the slow kinetics of the negative feedback loop essential in stabilizing these networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing the dependence of network stability on feedback time constant in Figure 12.

claim: Low-frequency perturbations (1/f noise) are pervasive across biological systems.
source: As low-frequency perturbations (1/f noise) are pervasive across biological systems, our analyses suggest a universal role for mechanisms that suppress low-frequency activity in stabilizing heterogeneous biological networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on 1/f noise in biological systems (Hausdorff and Peng, 1996; Gilden, 2001; Gisiger, 2001; Ward, 2001; Buzsaki, 2006).

claim: Mechanisms that suppress low-frequency activity have a universal role in stabilizing heterogeneous biological networks.
source: As low-frequency perturbations (1/f noise) are pervasive across biological systems, our analyses suggest a universal role for mechanisms that suppress low-frequency activity in stabilizing heterogeneous biological networks.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the study's findings and inference from the pervasiveness of low-frequency perturbations.

claim: Biological systems exhibit ubiquitous parametric variability spanning different scales of organization.
source: Biological systems exhibit ubiquitous parametric variability spanning different scales of organization, quantified through statistical heterogeneities in the underlying parameters.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations (Turrigiano and Nelson, 2000; Edelman and Gally, 2001; Maslov and Sneppen, 2002; Stelling et al., 2004; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Barkai and Shilo, 2007; Kitano, 2007; Félix and Barkoulas, 2015).

claim: Biological networks achieve stable outputs despite large-scale heterogeneities.
source: Strikingly, in spite of such large-scale heterogeneities, outputs of biological networks are stable and are precisely tuned to meet physiological demands.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about biological network stability.

claim: The continuous attractor network framework has been implicated in the generation of patterned neuronal activity in grid cells of the medial entorhinal cortex.
source: In this study, we quantitatively address questions on the impact of distinct forms of biological heterogeneities on the functional stability of a two-dimensional continuous attractor network (CAN), which has been implicated in the generation of patterned neuronal activity in grid cells of the medial entorhinal cortex (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Knierim and Zhang, 2012; Couey et al., 2013; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Yoon et al., 2013; Tukker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The fundamental question on the stability of 2D CAN models in the presence of biological heterogeneities remains unexplored.
source: Although the continuous attractor framework has offered insights about information encoding across several neural circuits (Samsonovich and McNaughton, 1997; Seung et al., 2000; Renart et al., 2003; Wills et al., 2005; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Knierim and Zhang, 2012; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Yoon et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017), the fundamental question on the stability of 2D CAN models in the presence of biological heterogeneities remains unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature that this study addresses.

claim: Virtual trajectories covered the entire arena with lesser time compared to real trajectories while not compromising on the accuracy of spatial activity maps.
source: Our analyses demonstrated the ability of virtual trajectories to cover the entire arena with lesser time (Figure 1A; Virtual trajectory), while not compromising on the accuracy of the spatial activity maps constructed from this trajectory in comparison to the maps obtained with the real trajectory (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The virtual trajectory covered similar areas in approximately six times lesser duration compared to the real trajectory.
source: Therefore, our virtual trajectory covered similar areas in approximately six times lesser duration (Figure 1A), which reduced the simulation duration by a factor of ~10 times when compared to the real rat trajectory, while yielding similar spatial activity maps (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The incorporation of any of the three forms of heterogeneities into the CAN model resulted in the disruption of grid pattern formation.
source: We found that the incorporation of any of the three forms of heterogeneities into the CAN model resulted in the disruption of grid pattern formation, with the deleterious impact increasing with increasing degree of heterogeneity (Figures 2E and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2E and 3.

claim: There was a hierarchy in the disruptive impact of different types of heterogeneities, with synaptic heterogeneity producing the largest reduction to grid score.
source: We found a hierarchy in the disruptive impact of different types of heterogeneities, with synaptic heterogeneity producing the largest reduction to grid score, followed by afferent heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of grid scores across different heterogeneity types shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Intrinsic heterogeneity was the least disruptive in the emergence of grid-cell activity.
source: Intrinsic heterogeneity was the least disruptive in the emergence of grid-cell activity, whereby a high degree of heterogeneity was required to hamper grid pattern formation (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: The introduction of the highest degree of all heterogeneities into the CAN model resulted in a complete loss of patterned activity and a marked reduction in the grid score values.
source: The introduction of the highest degree of all heterogeneities into the CAN model resulted in a complete loss of patterned activity and a marked reduction in the grid score values of all neurons in the network (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: The introduction of heterogeneities did not result in marked population-wide changes to broad measures such as average firing rate, mean size of grid fields and average grid spacing.
source: Detailed quantitative analysis of grid-cell activity showed that the introduction of heterogeneities did not result in marked population-wide changes to broad measures such as average firing rate, mean size of grid fields and average grid spacing (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The introduction of parametric heterogeneities resulted in a loss of spatial selectivity and disruption of patterned activity, reflected as progressive reductions in grid score, peak firing rate, information rate and sparsity.
source: Instead, the introduction of parametric heterogeneities resulted in a loss of spatial selectivity and disruption of patterned activity, reflected as progressive reductions in grid score, peak firing rate, information rate and sparsity (Figures 2–3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2–3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The disruptive impact of heterogeneities on grid-patterned activity was consistent across all tested network sizes.
source: We found that the disruptive impact of heterogeneities on grid-patterned activity was consistent across all tested networks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), manifesting as a reduction in grid score with increased degree of heterogeneities (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: The disruptive impact of heterogeneities on grid-patterned activity increased with increase in network size.
source: Our results also showed that the disruptive impact of heterogeneities on grid-patterned activity increased with increase in network size.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The incorporation of biological heterogeneities into networks disrupted their functional outcomes by introducing perturbations predominantly in the lower frequencies.
source: Strikingly, we found that the impact of introducing biological heterogeneities predominantly altered lower frequency components of neural activity, with little to no impact on higher frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The variance in the deviation of neural activity from the homogenous network progressively increased with higher degrees of heterogeneities, with large deviations occurring in the lower frequencies.
source: In addition, the variance in the deviation of neural activity from the homogenous network progressively increased with higher degrees of heterogeneities, with large deviations occurring in the lower frequencies (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Intrinsic resonance in neurons is mediated by the expression of resonating conductances endowed with specific biophysical characteristics.
source: We recognized intrinsic neuronal resonance as an established biological mechanism that suppresses low-frequency components, effectuated by the expression of resonating conductances endowed with specific biophysical characteristics (Hutcheon and Yarom, 2000; Narayanan and Johnston, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons in the superficial layers of the medial entorhinal cortex manifest resonance in the theta frequency range (4–10 Hz).
source: More specifically, excitatory (Erchova et al., 2004; Giocomo et al., 2007; Nolan et al., 2007; Garden et al., 2008; Pastoll et al., 2012) and inhibitory neurons (Boehlen et al., 2016) in the superficial layers of the medial entorhinal cortex manifest resonance in the theta frequency range (4–10 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The emergence of grid-patterned activity was not affected by replacing all the integrator neurons in the homogeneous CAN model with theta-frequency resonators.
source: We confirmed that the emergence of grid-patterned activity was not affected by replacing all the integrator neurons in the homogeneous CAN model with theta-frequency resonators (either phenomenological or mechanistic).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 10.

claim: Intrinsic neuronal resonance stabilized heterogeneous neural networks through suppression of low-frequency components of neural activity.
source: We systematically incorporated different forms of biological heterogeneities into the 2D resonator CAN model and found that intrinsic neuronal resonance stabilized heterogeneous neural networks, through suppression of low-frequency components of neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 8, 11, and 13.

claim: The mechanistic resonator was extremely effective in suppressing low-frequency activity without introducing spurious high-frequency components into neural activity.
source: Although this stabilization was observed with both phenomenological and mechanistic resonator networks, the mechanistic resonator was extremely effective in suppressing low-frequency activity without introducing spurious high-frequency components into neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative spectral analysis data shown in Figure 13.

claim: CAN models with resonators were able to reliably and robustly produce grid-patterned neural activity.
source: We found that CAN models with resonators were able to reliably and robustly produce grid-patterned neural activity, which were qualitatively (Figure 6A,B) and quantitatively (Figure 6C–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) similar to patterns produced by networks of integrator neurons across different values of τ.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increase in τ markedly increased spacing between grid fields and their average size, consequently reducing the number of grid fields within the arena.
source: Importantly, increase in τ markedly increased spacing between grid fields (Figure 6D) and their average size (Figure 6E), consequently reducing the number of grid fields within the arena (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, 6E, and 6F.

claim: The changes in grid spacing and size are not a result of change in resonance frequency, but a consequence of altered τ.
source: Within our model framework, it is important to emphasize that although increasing τ reduced fR in resonator neurons (Figures 5E and 6B), the changes in grid spacing and size are not a result of change in fR, but a consequence of altered τ.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of integrator and resonator networks shown in Figure 6.

claim: Altering the HPF exponent ε did not markedly change grid field patterns, grid score, average grid spacing, mean size, number, or sparsity of grid fields.
source: Specifically, when we fixed τ, and altered ε across resonator neurons in the homogeneous CAN model, fR of individual neurons changed (Figure 7A), but did not markedly change grid field patterns (Figure 7A), grid score, average grid spacing, mean size, number, or sparsity of grid fields (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: The presence of resonating neurons in the CAN model stabilized grid-patterned activity in individual neurons, despite the introduction of the highest degrees of all forms of biological heterogeneities.
source: Strikingly, we observed that the presence of resonating neurons in the CAN model stabilized grid-patterned activity in individual neurons, despite the introduction of the highest degrees of all forms of biological heterogeneities (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: With the incorporation of biological heterogeneities in resonator neuron networks, the imprecise shapes and stable patterns of grid-patterned firing tend closer to those of biologically observed grid cells.
source: However, that with the incorporation of biological heterogeneities in resonator neuron networks, the imprecise shapes and stable patterns of grid-patterned firing (e.g., Figure 8A) tend closer to those of biologically observed grid cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with biological data and the patterns shown in Figure 8A.

claim: All quantitative measurements of grid-cell activity were remarkably robust to the introduction of heterogeneities in resonator networks.
source: Quantitatively, we computed grid-cell measurements across all the 3600 neurons in the network and found that all quantitative measurements (Figure 8B–I, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), including the grid score (Figure 8B) and information rate (Figure 8H), were remarkably robust to the introduction of heterogeneities (cf. Figures 2–3 for CAN models with integrator neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B–I and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intrinsic resonance, introduced either through phenomenological or through mechanistic single-neuron models, yielded stable and robust grid-like pattern in heterogeneous CAN models.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that intrinsic neuronal resonance, introduced either through phenomenological (Figure 8) or through mechanistic (Figure 11) single-neuron models, yielded stable and robust grid-like pattern in heterogeneous CAN models.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 8 and 11.

claim: Homogenous CAN models built of integrators or resonators yielded stable closed orbit trajectories in phase plane representation.
source: This visual representation confirmed that homogenous CAN models built of integrators or resonators yielded stable closed orbit trajectories, representing similarly robust grid-patterned periodic activity (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phase plane analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The phase-plane plots of diagonal activity profiles from the heterogeneous integrator network lacked closed orbits.
source: Upon introduction of heterogeneities, the phase-plane plots of diagonal activity profiles from the heterogeneous integrator network lacked closed orbits (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phase plane analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The phase-plane plots from the heterogeneous resonator network manifested closed orbits even with the highest degree of heterogeneities introduced.
source: In striking contrast, the phase-plane plots from the heterogeneous resonator network manifested closed orbits even with the highest degree of heterogeneities introduced, irrespective of whether resonance was introduced through a phenomenological or a mechanistic model (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phase plane analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Heterogeneous CAN networks with neurons endowed with fast negative feedback loops were incapable of stabilizing the grid-cell network.
source: To the contrary, we found that heterogeneous CAN networks with neurons endowed with fast negative feedback loops were incapable of stabilizing the grid-cell network (Figure 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12.

claim: With progressive increase in τm, the grid-patterned firing stabilized even for high degrees of heterogeneities.
source: With progressive increase in τm, the grid-patterned firing stabilized even for high degrees of heterogeneities (Figure 12B,C for low values of τm; Figure 11B for τm = 75 ms), thus providing a direct additional line of evidence supporting our hypothesis on the need for targeted suppression of low-frequency components in stabilizing the network.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12B, 12C, and Figure 11B.

claim: Altering τm did not alter grid-patterned activity in homogeneous resonator networks.
source: We noted that the impact of altering τm was specifically related to stabilizing heterogeneous networks by suppressing heterogeneities-driven low-frequency perturbations because altering τm did not alter grid-patterned activity in homogeneous resonator networks (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9A and 9B.

claim: The variance in the deviations of neural activity in heterogeneous networks with reference to the respective homogeneous models were considerably lower with resonator neurons compared to their integrator counterparts.
source: First, we found that the variance in the deviations of neural activity in heterogeneous networks with reference to the respective homogeneous models were considerably lower with resonator neurons (both phenomenological and mechanistic models), compared to their integrator counterparts (Figure 13A,B, Figure 13D,E, Figure 13—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 13 and Figure 13—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Networks with resonators suppressed lower frequencies (predominantly the 0–2 Hz band) and enhanced power in the range of neuronal resonance frequencies, when compared with their integrator counterparts.
source: Second, comparing the relative power of neural activity across different octaves, we found that network with resonators suppressed lower frequencies (predominantly the 0–2 Hz band) and enhanced power in the range of neuronal resonance frequencies, when compared with their integrator counterparts (Figure 13C, Figure 13F, Figure 13—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by octave analysis data shown in Figure 13C, 13F, and Figure 13—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The phenomenological resonators were built with a simple HPF that is not endowed with activity-dependent filtering capabilities.
source: The phenomenological resonators were built with a simple HPF that is not endowed with activity-dependent filtering capabilities.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction method.

claim: The derivative-based implementation of the phenomenological resonator model yielded spurious high-frequency power.
source: In addition, the derivative-based implementation of the phenomenological resonator model yielded spurious high-frequency power, which was averted with the slow activity-dependent negative feedback loop incorporated into the mechanistic resonator model (Figure 13D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative spectral analysis shown in Figure 13D–F.

claim: Intrinsic neuronal resonance constitutes a cellular-scale activity-dependent negative feedback mechanism.
source: Our analyses suggest that intrinsic neuronal resonance constitutes a cellular-scale activity-dependent negative feedback mechanism, a specific instance of a well-established network motif that effectuates stability and suppresses perturbations across different biological networks (Savageau, 1974; Becskei and Serrano, 2000; Thattai and van Oudenaarden, 2001; Austin et al., 2006; Dublanche et al., 2006; Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008; Lestas et al., 2010; Cheong et al., 2011; Voliotis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and supported by citations to literature on negative feedback mechanisms.

claim: Resonating conductances have been implicated in providing frequency selectivity to specific range of frequencies under sub- and supra-threshold conditions.
source: Resonating conductances have been implicated in providing frequency selectivity to specific range of frequencies under sub- and supra-threshold conditions (Hutcheon and Yarom, 2000; Narayanan and Johnston, 2007; Hu et al., 2009; Das and Narayanan, 2017; Das et al., 2017), in mediating membrane potential oscillations (Fransén et al., 2004; Mittal and Narayanan, 2018), in mediating coincidence detection through alteration to the class of neural excitability (Das and Narayanan, 2017; Das et al., 2017), in regulating spatio-temporal summation of synaptic inputs (Garden et al., 2008), in introducing phase leads in specific ranges of frequencies regulating temporal relationships of neural responses to oscillatory inputs (Narayanan and Johnston, 2008), in regulating local-field potentials and associated spike phases (Sinha and Narayanan, 2015; Ness et al., 2018), in mediating activity homeostasis through regulation of neural excitability (Brager and Johnston, 2007; Narayanan and Johnston, 2007; Honnuraiah and Narayanan, 2013), in altering synaptic plasticity profiles (Nolan et al., 2007; Narayanan and Johnston, 2010), and in regulating grid-cell scales (Giocomo et al., 2007; Giocomo et al., 2011b; Giocomo et al., 2011a; Pastoll et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on resonating conductances.

claim: The specific resonance frequency of a given neural structure is a reflection of the need to suppress frequencies where the perturbations are introduced by specific forms and degree of biological heterogeneities expressed in the network where the structure resides.
source: A corollary to this postulate is that the specific resonance frequency of a given neural structure is a reflection of the need to suppress frequencies where the perturbations are introduced by specific forms and degree of biological heterogeneities expressed in the network where the structure resides.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Negative feedback is a standard motif for establishing stabilization and robustness of dynamical systems spanning control engineering and biological networks.
source: From a broader perspective, negative feedback is a standard motif for establishing stabilization and robustness of dynamical systems spanning control engineering (Nyquist, 1932; Black, 1934; Bode, 1945; Bechhoefer, 2005; Åström and Murray, 2008) and biological networks (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Weng et al., 1999; Hutcheon and Yarom, 2000; Bhalla et al., 2002; Milo et al., 2002; Shen-Orr et al., 2002; Tyson et al., 2003; Alon, 2007; Turrigiano, 2007; Novák and Tyson, 2008; Tyson and Novák, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on negative feedback in engineering and biology.

claim: Negative feedback has been shown to reduce the effects of noise and enhance system stability with reference to internal and external perturbations.
source: Importantly, with specific relevance to our hypothesis, negative feedback has been shown to reduce the effects of noise and enhance system stability with reference to internal and external perturbations because of the suppressive nature of this motif (Savageau, 1974; Becskei and Serrano, 2000; Thattai and van Oudenaarden, 2001; Austin et al., 2006; Dublanche et al., 2006; Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008; Lestas et al., 2010; Cheong et al., 2011; Voliotis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on negative feedback and noise reduction.

claim: The dynamics of action potential is critically dependent on the negative feedback by delayed-rectifier potassium channels.
source: At the cellular scale, the dynamics of action potential, which is a fundamental unit of information transfer in nervous system, is critically dependent on the negative feedback by delayed-rectifier potassium channels (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952c; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952b; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the classic Hodgkin-Huxley papers.

claim: Resonating conductances mediate slow negative feedback in sustaining sub-threshold membrane potential oscillations along with amplifying conductances that mediate a fast positive feedback loop.
source: Resonating conductances (or phenomenological inductances) mediate slow negative feedback in sustaining sub-threshold membrane potential oscillations along with amplifying conductances that mediate a fast positive feedback loop (Cole and Baker, 1941; Mauro, 1961; Cole, 1968; Mauro et al., 1970; Hutcheon and Yarom, 2000; Narayanan and Johnston, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on resonating conductances and oscillations.

claim: Rate-based models are inherently limited in their ability to assess temporal relationships between spike timings.
source: Our analyses here employed a rate-based CAN model for the generation of grid-patterned activity. Rate-based models are inherently limited in their ability to assess temporal relationships between spike timings, which are important from the temporal coding perspective where spike timings with reference to extracellular oscillations have been shown to carry spatial information within grid fields (Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the modeling approach, supported by a citation.

claim: The CAN model is one of several theoretical and computational frameworks that have been proposed for the emergence of grid-cell activity patterns.
source: Additionally, the CAN model is one of the several theoretical and computational frameworks that have been proposed for the emergence of grid-cell activity patterns, and there are lines of experimental evidence that support aspects of these distinct models (Kropff and Treves, 2008; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2011; Giocomo et al., 2011a; Navratilova et al., 2012; Couey et al., 2013; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Yoon et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2017; Urdapilleta et al., 2017; Stella et al., 2020; Tukker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to different theoretical frameworks for grid cells.

claim: The rate-based CAN model was adopted from Burak and Fiete, 2009.
source: The rate-based CAN model consisting of a 2D neural sheet (default size: 60 × 60 = 3600 neurons) with the default integrator neurons for eliciting grid-cell activity was adopted from Burak and Fiete, 2009.
evidence: This is a statement about the source of the model used in the study.

claim: The sides of the neural sheet were connected, yielding a toroidal (or periodic) network configuration.
source: The sides of this neural sheet were connected, yielding a toroidal (or periodic) network configuration.
evidence: This is a description of the network topology used in the model.

claim: Each neuron in the CAN model received two distinct sets of synaptic inputs: one from other neurons within the network and another feed-forward afferent input that was dependent on the velocity of the virtual animal.
source: Each neuron in the CAN model received two distinct sets of synaptic inputs, one from other neurons within the network and another feed-forward afferent input that was dependent on the velocity of the virtual animal.
evidence: This is a description of the inputs to neurons in the model.

claim: The real trajectory spanned 590 s of real-world time and required considerable simulation time to sufficiently explore the entire arena.
source: However, the real trajectory spanned 590 s of real-world time and required considerable simulation time to sufficiently explore the entire arena, essential for computing high-resolution spatial activity maps.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational requirements of using real trajectories.

claim: The correlation values between the spatial autocorrelation of rate maps of individual grid cells for real trajectory and that from the virtual trajectory at different rat runtimes were high across all measured runtimes.
source: Specifically, the correlation values between the spatial autocorrelation of rate maps of individual grid cells for real trajectory and that from the virtual trajectory at different rat runtimes (Trun) were high across all measured runtimes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no substantial improvement in accuracy beyond Trun = 100 s.
source: As there was no substantial improvement in accuracy beyond Trun = 100 s, we employed Trun = 100 s for all simulations (compared to the 590 s of the real trajectory).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Grid score was computed by assessing rotational symmetry in the spatial rate map.
source: Grid score was computed by assessing rotational symmetry in the spatial rate map.
evidence: This is a description of the method used to compute grid score.
